all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` claims sandboxed fix verification, but the optional test command is executed without rewriting file arguments into sandbox paths. In `evaluate_fix()`, the patched file is created under `tmpdir` via `_create_sandbox(...)`, then tests run as `_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)`. If `test_cmd` contains explicit repo-relative or absolute paths—as the live caller in `immune_agents.py` does (`["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]`)—pytest resolves against the original tree, not the patched sandbox copy. Evidence: only `cwd` is changed; command arguments are passed unchanged. This makes the core “does the proposed fix break anything?” capability test the real source tree, not the patched candidate.
FOLLOW: Downstream, fix evaluation can mark a fix SAFE/NEUTRAL even when sandbox tests would fail against the patched code, or HARMFUL for failures unrelated to the patch. In the immune pipeline, SAFE/NEUTRAL sets `finding.verified = True`, which activates the bug-closed gate and suppresses future findings as duplicates of a supposedly verified fix. That can silently close still-broken bugs and mislead human reviewers about end-to-end status.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — before running tests, rewrite any file/directory arguments in `test_cmd` that point into the source tree so they point to the corresponding paths under `tmpdir`, then execute the rewritten command.

all_findings.description:
FIND — fix evaluation compares pre-fix diagnostics on the original file against post-fix diagnostics on the sandboxed file, but both are single-file tool runs. `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` and later `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, patched_path)` invoke pyright/ruff/bandit on only one file. For pyright/mypy especially, diagnostics depend on package context and import graph; the module docstring for `_create_sandbox()` explicitly acknowledges that flat single-file analysis causes spurious import errors. The sandbox preserves full structure, but the tool counts still only inspect the patched file path, not the copied source set as a project-consistent run.
FOLLOW: A fix can change imports, symbols, or cross-file contracts and still appear SAFE because only local diagnostics are counted. Conversely, path/context differences between original single-file and sandbox single-file runs can produce meaningless deltas. Since SAFE/NEUTRAL drives `verified=True`, this can silently certify bad fixes and close bugs prematurely.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — compute both pre- and post-fix baselines by running each tool over the full mirrored source file set, using the original source set for baseline and the sandbox source set for post-fix, then compare counts attributable to the whole project run.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` records line/column directly from pyright JSON start positions without converting from pyright’s 0-based coordinates. Code: `line=rng.get("line", 0)`, `column=rng.get("character", 0)`. Pyright’s `range.start.line` and `character` are 0-based in `--outputjson` output. The rest of the module and surrounding system use human line numbers conventionally as 1-based (`bandit` and parsed `mypy` diagnostics already are).
FOLLOW: Health scan locations are silently off by one for pyright findings. Any consumer surfacing these coordinates to reviewers or using them for follow-up lookup will mispoint diagnostics, degrading the health scan’s practical usefulness and potentially causing false “citation mismatch” reasoning elsewhere.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — add 1 to pyright `line` and `character` when constructing `ToolDiagnostic`, while preserving 0 only for missing/unknown coordinates.

all_findings.description:
FIND — the advertised “defect detection” feature is not actually implemented as a distinct capability. The module header and focus state function 2 is “Defect detection — classify findings by defect category,” but there is no public function that takes findings or tool diagnostics and performs the promised defect-detection stage; only per-tool inline categorisers exist during scan parsing. No coordinator method exposes “defect detection” output separate from raw scan aggregation.
FOLLOW: This is a dead feature claim in a PoC module that the insect brain may rely on conceptually. Reviewers expecting a distinct defect-detection signal will not get one, and future callers have no API to invoke the advertised function 2. The module partially works, but one of its declared end-to-end features never fires.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — add a small public function that accepts collected `ToolDiagnostic` items and returns grouped diagnostics/counts by `DefectCategory`, and call it from `scan_health()` or `EndocrineLayer.run()` so function 2 exists as an actual emitted result.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` uses `sorted(durations)[len(durations) // 2]` and the same pattern for response sizes, which is not the statistical median for even-length lists; it selects the upper middle element. With 4 models this inflates the baseline and suppresses slow-model / large-response detection. In this system there are 5 models today, but the code is generic and the topology/history includes model failure handling, so active model count can become even.
FOLLOW: After one model failure, pacing thresholds can become systematically too lax, delaying or suppressing pacing signals exactly when degraded operation makes them more valuable. This does not crash the PoC but can make convergence/pacing guidance silently less responsive.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — use `statistics.median()` for durations and response sizes instead of upper-middle indexing.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` claims to sandbox-test proposed fixes, but the optional test command is executed unchanged inside the tempdir (`_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)`) without rewriting any file arguments to the sandbox tree. In the actual caller shown in `immune_agents.py`, the command is `["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]`. That path is relative to the real repo, not the sandbox copy. The sandbox only contains copied source files, not `bench/tests/`, and any absolute paths in test commands would still target the real workspace. Evidence: `evaluate_fix()` creates a temp tree via `_create_sandbox(...)`, but never remaps `test_cmd` paths nor copies tests into the sandbox.
FOLLOW: Downstream, the advertised “sandbox-test proposed fixes” feature does not actually validate the patched code under test. Best case, tests fail spuriously because the requested test path does not exist under `tmpdir`; worst case, if the command uses absolute paths or module discovery from the parent environment, tests execute against the unpatched real tree, producing false SAFE/NEUTRAL verdicts. That directly undermines the fix-verification gate used by the immune pipeline to mark findings `verified=True`, so bugs can be marked closed based on tests that never exercised the patch.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — when creating the sandbox, also copy the test targets needed by `test_cmd` and rewrite any source/test path arguments in `test_cmd` from real paths to their sandbox equivalents before invoking the subprocess. If path rewriting cannot be done reliably, skip tests and mark them not run rather than pretending they were sandboxed.

all_findings.description:
FIND — pre-fix and post-fix tool counts are measured on different analysis scopes. `evaluate_fix()` computes baselines with `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` / `run_ruff(target_path)` / `run_bandit(target_path)` on the real single file, then computes post-fix counts on `patched_path` inside a sandbox that preserves the package structure and may change import resolution. The module comment explicitly says preserving structure matters because flat single-file analysis causes spurious import errors. Evidence: `_create_sandbox()` exists specifically to preserve package layout for post-fix runs, but no equivalent sandboxed baseline is used.
FOLLOW: Verdicts compare unlike quantities. A harmless fix can look HARMFUL because the post-fix run sees package-import context that the baseline did not, or a harmful fix can look SAFE because the single-file baseline already masked package-dependent diagnostics. This corrupts the key SAFE/HARMFUL decision used to close findings.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — compute pre-fix baselines in the same sandboxed project layout as post-fix, using an unmodified copy of the target and identical tool invocation scope.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_count_tool_issues()` collapses all tool failures to zero issues by `except Exception: return 0`. That includes missing binaries, timeouts, parse failures, invocation errors, and invalid output. `evaluate_fix()` then treats those zero counts as real measurements. Evidence: `_count_tool_issues()` catches all exceptions; `_run_tool()` encodes timeout/not-found as synthetic CompletedProcess values; tool parsers often return empty lists on parse failure instead of surfacing an error.
FOLLOW: The fix-evaluation feature silently fails open. If pyright/ruff/bandit are unavailable or erroring, both pre and post counts become zero and many patches get NEUTRAL or SAFE instead of UNEVALUABLE. The immune pipeline then may set `verified=True` on fixes that were never actually checked by tools.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — make `_count_tool_issues()` return an explicit failure state (e.g. `None`) on tool execution/parsing failure, and have `evaluate_fix()` mark the result `UNEVALUABLE` if any required tool could not be measured.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` only treats `stderr == "NOT_FOUND"` as fatal. Timeouts from `_run_tool()` are returned as `CompletedProcess(..., stderr="TIMEOUT")`, but `run_pyright()` then attempts to parse empty `stdout`, logs a warning, and returns `[]`. `run_ruff()` and `run_bandit()` have the same fail-open pattern for timeout/other malformed output. Evidence: `_run_tool()` returns sentinel stderr strings; the runners only special-case NOT_FOUND.
FOLLOW: Health scans and fix evaluations silently under-report diagnostics when tools hang or emit bad output. That can make health look clean and can mark fixes SAFE/NEUTRAL when the checker simply timed out. This is silently wrong output in one of the module’s core functions.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — treat `stderr == "TIMEOUT"` and non-parseable output from a tool invocation as tool failure, not as zero diagnostics; surface that in `tools_available`/evaluation state so the caller can mark the scan or fix evaluation incomplete.

all_findings.description:
FIND — the coordinator interface does not implement the documented “defect detect” capability as a callable feature. The file header lists four core functions including “Defect detect — classify findings by defect category”, but the public API only exposes `scan_health`, `evaluate_fix(es)`, `compute_pacing_signals`, and `EndocrineLayer.run()`. Category classification exists only as an internal side effect inside tool-specific runners; there is no standalone defect-detection function for arbitrary findings/diagnostics. Evidence: no public function or report field corresponding to function 2 beyond embedded `category` strings.
FOLLOW: One of the advertised endocrine features never fires independently. Any caller expecting a separate defect-detection stage cannot invoke it, and the brain receives only raw health-scan categories, not a dedicated defect-classification output. For a PoC that claims end-to-end feature coverage, this is dead/missing functionality.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — add a simple public `detect_defects(diagnostics: List[ToolDiagnostic]) -> Dict[str, int] | List[ToolDiagnostic]` wrapper that exposes the already-derived categories, and include its result explicitly in the endocrine report if the brain depends on it.

all_findings.description:
FIND — slow-model and large-response pacing thresholds use `sorted(values)[len(values) // 2]`, which is the upper middle element for even-sized sets rather than the statistical median. With 5 models this is usually fine, but the code accepts arbitrary lists and can mis-threshold when model count changes or failures reduce the list to an even cardinality. Evidence: `compute_pacing_signals()` uses this pattern for both durations and response chars.
FOLLOW: Pacing signals can trigger too aggressively or not at all around threshold boundaries, causing the insect brain to emit misleading `increase_timeout` / `degrade_relay` actions. This is quality degradation rather than total breakage, but it directly affects pacing decisions.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — use `statistics.median()` for duration and response-size baselines.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `scan_health()` reports empty `tools_available` when `source_paths` contains no existing files. It returns early with `HealthScan(elapsed_s=...)` before initializing tool availability for the known tool set. Evidence: early return occurs before the tool loop populates availability keys.
FOLLOW: The report cannot distinguish “no files to scan” from “tool availability unknown”, and downstream consumers expecting fixed keys for pyright/ruff/bandit/mypy get an incomplete interface. This weakens health telemetry and can break simple consumers that index those keys directly.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — on the no-files early return, populate `tools_available` with all known tools set to `False` or a consistent sentinel state.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_find_target_file()` falls back to `source_paths[0]` whenever it cannot resolve a path from the finding description/fix. In a multi-file review batch, an unresolved finding is therefore evaluated against an arbitrary first file. Evidence: final line of `_find_target_file()` returns the first source path if any exist.
FOLLOW: Fix evaluation can patch and lint the wrong file while still returning a concrete verdict. That produces silently wrong SAFE/HARMFUL results and wrong `original_file` attribution for findings whose descriptions lack an exact path mention.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — if no target file can be resolved uniquely, return `None` and mark the evaluation `UNEVALUABLE` instead of defaulting to the first source file.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_count_tool_issues` passes a single string path to tool runners that expect `List[str]`. Lines ~370-372: `run_pyright([file_path])` is correct inside the helper, but the caller at lines ~340-342 calls `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` where `target_path` is a string. Inside `_count_tool_issues`, `tool_runner([file_path])` wraps it in a list — this is correct. However, the pre-fix baseline at lines ~340-342 runs tools on the original file on disk, not in the sandbox. The post-fix analysis at lines ~365-367 runs tools on `patched_path` which is inside the tmpdir. The problem: `run_pyright`, `run_ruff`, `run_bandit` receive `[patched_path]` — a file inside a tmpdir with no `__init__.py` files for sibling packages, and potentially broken import resolution because only `source_paths` files are copied but their transitive dependencies (e.g., `bench.dm._types`) are not. This means post-fix tool runs will produce spurious import errors that inflate `new_type_errors` / `new_ruff_errors`, making nearly every fix appear HARMFUL.
FOLLOW: This is the core capability of the endocrine layer — fix evaluation. If post-fix analysis always produces spurious errors, the net_type_errors will almost always be positive, and `_compute_fix_verdict` returns HARMFUL. The immune pipeline (Stage 4 in `immune_agents.py` lines calling `evaluate_fixes`) uses the verdict to set `finding.verified = True` only for SAFE/NEUTRAL. If all fixes evaluate as HARMFUL due to spurious import errors, the bug-closed gate never fires, and findings churn indefinitely across rounds. This is a silent correctness failure — the feature appears to work but produces wrong results.
all_findings.proposed_fix: In `_create_sandbox`, after copying source_paths, walk up from the common ancestor looking for `__init__.py` files and copy them too. Alternatively (simpler for PoC): run post-fix tools with `--pythonpath` or equivalent flags pointing to the project root. Simplest fix: add the original project root to the sandbox's tool invocations by passing `cwd` to `_run_tool` or adding `--pythonpath` to pyright/mypy. For pyright specifically, create a minimal `pyrightconfig.json` in the tmpdir with `"extraPaths"` pointing to the original project root.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_apply_fix_to_source` Strategy 2 (whole-file replacement) has a dangerous heuristic: if a proposed fix compiles as valid Python and has ≥5 lines, it replaces the entire source file. Model-generated `proposed_fix` fields routinely contain valid Python (e.g., a corrected function definition with imports and docstrings). A 6-line function fix that happens to compile will replace a 1000-line source file with just those 6 lines. The `compile()` check at line ~295 succeeds for any syntactically valid Python fragment.
FOLLOW: When Strategy 2 triggers incorrectly, the patched file in the sandbox contains only the fix fragment. Post-fix tool analysis then sees massive regressions (hundreds of missing symbols), producing a HARMFUL verdict. This compounds F001 — even if F001 were fixed, this would still produce false HARMFUL verdicts for any multi-line proposed fix that happens to be valid Python. Worse: if the fix text is a complete module (copy-pasted with the fix applied), the replacement is correct — so the heuristic must distinguish "complete replacement" from "function fragment". Currently it cannot.

FIND — `_compute_fix_verdict` checks each tool dimension independently (good), but the SAFE path has a logic gap. If `net_type_errors == 0` AND `net_ruff_errors == 0` AND `net_bandit_issues == 0` AND `tests_passed is None` (not run), the function falls through to return NEUTRAL. But `total_net` is 0 and `tests_passed` is None, so neither the `total_net < 0` branch (SAFE) nor the `tests_passed is True` branch (SAFE) fires. A fix that introduces zero new issues and removes zero issues, with no tests, is NEUTRAL — which means the finding is NOT marked as verified. This is the most common case: most fixes will not change aggregate lint counts (they fix a logic bug, not a lint issue), and most evaluations won't have a test command.
FOLLOW: If the typical fix evaluation returns NEUTRAL, and the immune pipeline's Stage 4 only marks findings as `verified=True` for SAFE/NEUTRAL verdicts — wait, re-reading `immune_agents.py` line in Stage 4: `if ev.verdict in ("SAFE", "NEUTRAL")` — NEUTRAL does trigger verification. So the finding still gets verified. However, the semantic intent is wrong: NEUTRAL should mean "fix had no measurable effect" (neither helpful nor harmful), while a fix that doesn't change lint counts but might fix a real logic bug should arguably be SAFE if it doesn't introduce new issues. This is a MEDIUM issue — the verdict is semantically misleading but doesn't block operation because NEUTRAL still triggers verification.
all_findings.proposed_fix: No code change needed for PoC — NEUTRAL triggers verification in the consumer. Document the semantic: NEUTRAL means "no measurable change in static analysis, no tests run" which correctly implies "not proven harmful."

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals` novelty plateau detection uses `all(n <= 1 for n in recent)` with `window = 3`. The threshold `<= 1` means a round with exactly 1 novel finding is treated as "plateau." In early rounds of a multi-model review with 5 models, 1 novel finding per round is not a plateau — it's active discovery. The signal fires too early, potentially triggering premature convergence checks via `suggested_action="check_convergence"`.
FOLLOW: The insect brain receives this pacing signal and may use it to influence convergence decisions. If the brain treats `check_convergence` as a strong signal, genuine productive rounds with 1 novel finding each could trigger early termination. In the context of a 5-model review producing ~10-20 findings per round in early rounds, this is unlikely to fire prematurely. But in later rounds where discovery rate naturally drops, `n=1` per round for 3 rounds IS a reasonable plateau signal. The threshold is defensible for later rounds but aggressive for early rounds.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
Add a round-index guard: only emit novelty plateau signal after a minimum number of rounds (e.g., round_idx >= 4). This prevents false plateau signals in early rounds while preserving the signal for genuine late-round plateaus.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix` runs pre-fix baselines on the original file path on disk via `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` (line ~340), then runs post-fix analysis on `patched_path` inside the sandbox (line ~365). These are different environments: the original file has full project context (sibling modules, `__init__.py`, config files), while the sandbox has only the files in `source_paths`. The baseline and post-fix counts are not comparable — they're measured in different contexts. A file that has 5 type errors in the full project might show 50 in the sandbox (missing imports), making `net_type_errors = +45` regardless of the fix quality.
FOLLOW: This is the same root cause as F001 but from a different angle. F001 describes the sandbox incompleteness; F005 describes the asymmetric measurement. Even if the sandbox were complete, measuring baseline on the original file and post-fix on the sandbox copy creates an apples-to-oranges comparison. The correct approach is to measure both baseline and post-fix in the same environment (both in the sandbox, or both on disk).
all_findings.proposed_fix:
Run pre-fix baselines inside the sandbox too. Create the sandbox with the unpatched file first, run baselines, then overwrite with the patched version and run post-fix analysis. This ensures both measurements use the same environment.
# Create sandbox with ORIGINAL file first for baseline

    try:

        eval_result.pre_ruff_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_ruff, original_sandbox_path)
        eval_result.pre_bandit_issues = _count_tool_issues(run_bandit, original_sandbox_path)

        # Now overwrite with patched version
        Path(original_sandbox_path).write_text(patched, encoding="utf-8")
        # ... post-fix analysis on same path ...

all_findings.description:
FIND — `EndocrineLayer._scan_history` grows unboundedly. Every call to `run()` appends a `HealthScan` (which contains the full list of `ToolDiagnostic` objects) to `_scan_history`. In a long experiment with many rounds, each HealthScan could contain hundreds of diagnostics with string fields. There is no eviction or windowing.
FOLLOW: `health_trend()` iterates all scans to build trends. For a PoC with ≤15 rounds and ≤4 source files, this is not a problem. The memory growth is O(rounds × diagnostics_per_round). At ~100 diagnostics per scan and ~15 rounds, this is ~1500 ToolDiagnostic objects — negligible. This is LOW priority at PoC stage.
all_findings.proposed_fix: No fix needed for PoC. If the system scales beyond ~50 rounds, add a sliding window to `_scan_history` (keep last N scans, aggregate older ones into counts only).

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_find_target_file` constructs `desc = finding.description + " " + finding.proposed_fix` and extracts file paths via regex `r"[\w/\\]+\.py\b"`. The regex is too permissive — it matches any word characters followed by `.py`, including fragments like `mypy`, `copy`, `scipy`. If a finding description mentions "run mypy" or "use scipy", the regex extracts `mypy` or `scipy` as candidate file paths, then attempts suffix-matching against source_paths. This is unlikely to produce a false positive match (no source path ends in `/mypy` or `/scipy`), but it wastes cycles and could produce unexpected matches if a source file happens to have a matching basename.
FOLLOW: The fallback is `source_paths[0]`, which is correct in most cases since the review typically targets a single file. The regex false-match risk is low in practice. MEDIUM priority.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Tighten the regex to require a path separator or start-of-word before the filename: `r"(?:^|[\s/\\])(\S+\.py)\b"`. Or simpler: require at least one `/` or `\` in the match to confirm it's a path, not a bare word.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals` has a defensive coercion for `context_budget` at lines ~455-460 that handles `dict`, `str`, `float` types. If `context_budget` is a dict, it takes `max(context_budget.values())`. This is a workaround for TOML config parsing quirks. However, if `context_budget` is a dict with string values (e.g., `{"CC2": "80000"}`), `max()` compares strings lexicographically, not numerically. `"9000" > "80000"` is True in string comparison.
FOLLOW: The TOML config parser should produce integer values for numeric fields. The defensive coercion exists because the caller (`EndocrineLayer.run`) passes `context_budget` as a plain `int` parameter. The dict case would only arise if someone passes the raw config dict instead of extracting the value. Low probability in practice.

FIND — `evaluate_fix` runs pre-fix baselines sequentially: pyright, ruff, bandit — three separate subprocess invocations on the original file. Then it creates the sandbox and runs all three again on the patched file. That's 6 sequential subprocess calls per fix evaluation, each with a 60-second timeout. With `max_evals=20`, that's up to 120 subprocess calls, potentially ~120 minutes wall time in the worst case (all timeouts).
FOLLOW: In practice, tool invocations on a single file take 1-5 seconds each, so 20 fixes × 6 calls × 3s ≈ 6 minutes. This is acceptable for PoC. The pacing signals will flag it if it's slow. Not a blocking issue.
all_findings.proposed_fix: No fix needed for PoC. Future optimization: run pre/post tools in parallel using ThreadPoolExecutor.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_mypy()` fails to parse mypy output when diagnostic spans multiple lines (contains newline). The regex pattern expects a single line (`^(.+?):(\d+):(\d+):\s+(error|warning|note):\s+(.+?)(?:\s+\[(.+?)\])?$`). If mypy emits a diagnostic with an embedded newline (e.g., long messages), the regex matches only the first line, dropping the remainder of the message and causing subsequent lines to be misparsed. This silently discards evidence and undercounts mypy diagnostics.  
FOLLOW: Health scan counts will be wrong, `counts_by_tool["mypy"]` undercounts, `counts_by_severity` wrong, downstream trend detection receives incorrect baseline. The insect brain may miss type‑safety defects that mypy reported.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX — Change `run_mypy()` to split the output on `\n` but treat each diagnostic line independently only if it matches the pattern; ignore non‑matching lines (they are continuation lines). Replace `for line in result.stdout.splitlines():` with a state machine that accumulates continuation lines.  
def run_mypy(paths: List[str]) -> List[ToolDiagnostic]:
    ...
    diagnostics = []
    current = None
    for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
        m = pattern.match(line)
        if m:
            # start a new diagnostic
            if current is not None:
                diagnostics.append(current)
            msg = m.group(5)
            code = m.group(6) or ""
            msg_lower = msg.lower()
            if "none" in msg_lower or "optional" in msg_lower:
                category = DefectCategory.NULL_DEREF
            else:
                category = DefectCategory.TYPE_SAFETY
            current = ToolDiagnostic(
                tool="mypy",
                file_path=m.group(1),
                line=int(m.group(2)),
                column=int(m.group(3)),
                code=code,
                message=msg,
                severity=m.group(4),
                category=category,
            )
        elif current is not None:
            # continuation line — append to message
            current.message += "\n" + line.strip()
    if current is not None:
        diagnostics.append(current)
    return diagnostics

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_find_target_file()` uses `os.sep` in suffix match (`sp_path.endswith(os.sep + match)`). On Windows, `os.sep` is `\`. The pattern extracted from description uses forward slash (`/`) because models write paths with `/`. The suffix match fails, causing fallback to basename match, which may pick the wrong file if multiple source files share the same basename. This leads to fix evaluation on the wrong file, producing incorrect `HARMFUL`/`SAFE` verdicts.  
FOLLOW: Wrong file evaluation → wrong net‑issue counts → wrong verdict (`HARMFUL` for a correct fix). The endocrine layer will flag correct fixes as harmful, causing the insect brain to ignore them; bugs remain unfixed.

FIND — `evaluate_fix()` calls `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, target_path)` on the original `target_path` (real source file) for baseline, but calls `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, patched_path)` on the sandboxed `patched_path`. If the sandbox environment lacks dependencies (e.g., third‑party imports), pyright will report import errors that are not present in the original file. This inflates `new_type_errors`, causing a `HARMFUL` verdict even when the fix introduces no actual type errors.  
FOLLOW: False `HARMFUL` verdicts → correct fixes rejected → bugs persist. The endocrine layer’s key capability (fix evaluation) is broken for any project with imports outside the sandbox.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX — Run baseline counts also in the sandbox (copy original file to sandbox, run tools there). In `evaluate_fix()`, create sandbox before baseline counts, copy original file to sandbox, compute baseline counts there, then patch and compute post‑fix counts in the same sandbox. This ensures identical environment.  
# In evaluate_fix, after determining target_path and reading source_text:
tmpdir = None
try:
    # Create sandbox with original file
    tmpdir, orig_sandbox_path = _create_sandbox(target_path, source_paths, source_text)
    # Baseline counts in sandbox
    eval_result.pre_type_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_pyright, orig_sandbox_path)
    eval_result.pre_ruff_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_ruff, orig_sandbox_path)
    eval_result.pre_bandit_issues = _count_tool_issues(run_bandit, orig_sandbox_path)
    # Apply fix to sandbox copy
    patched = _apply_fix_to_source(source_text, finding.proposed_fix)
    if patched is None:
        ...
    # Write patched version over the sandbox file
    Path(orig_sandbox_path).write_text(patched, encoding="utf-8")
    # Post‑fix counts in same sandbox
    eval_result.new_type_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_pyright, orig_sandbox_path)
    eval_result.new_ruff_errors = _count_tool_issues(run_ruff, orig_sandbox_path)
    eval_result.new_bandit_issues = _count_tool_issues(run_bandit, orig_sandbox_path)
    ... # rest unchanged

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_count_tool_issues()` catches `Exception` and returns 0. If a tool crashes (e.g., pyright segfault), the function returns 0, making it appear that the file has zero issues. This masks tool failures and leads to incorrect net‑issue calculation (e.g., `net_type_errors = 0 - 0 = 0`), potentially marking a harmful fix as `SAFE`.  
FOLLOW: Tool crashes are silent; the endocrine layer reports false cleanliness; harmful fixes may be accepted because the crash hides introduced errors.

FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` does not guard against division‑by‑zero when `context_budget` is 0. The line `context_fraction = cumulative_context_chars / context_budget` will raise `ZeroDivisionError`. This crashes the endocrine layer, stopping all pacing signals. The insect brain receives no pacing signals for the round.  
FOLLOW: Endocrine crash → no pacing signals → insect brain misses context‑growth warnings; may exceed budget without degradation.

FIND — `_apply_fix_to_source()` line‑range replacement logic is broken for multi‑line ranges. When `start_line != end_line`, it joins the block as a single string, replaces `old_frag` with `new_frag`, then assigns the entire new block to `lines[start_line:end_line + 1]`. This replaces N lines with 1 line, changing line numbers for all subsequent code. This corrupts the file and will cause tool errors (line mismatches).  
FOLLOW: Corrupted sandbox file → pyright/ruff report errors on wrong lines → fix evaluation verdict based on corrupt analysis.

FIND — `_apply_fix_to_source()`’s search‑replace pattern (`replace ... with ...`) uses `re.DOTALL` but matches greedily across the entire fix text; if the fix contains multiple such patterns, only the first is applied. The pattern should apply all replacements described in the fix.  
FOLLOW: Partial fix application → sandbox file only partially patched → evaluation tests wrong code, may reject a correct fix because it wasn’t fully applied.

FIND — `scan_health()` runs all four tools sequentially even if a tool is already known unavailable (from `tools_available` dict). The loop `for tool_name, runner in [("pyright", run_pyright), ...]` calls `runner(existing)`, which will raise `ToolNotFoundError` again (already caught earlier). This wastes time re‑raising and catching the same exception.  
FOLLOW: Unnecessary repeated exception handling; slight performance penalty each round.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX — Skip tools already marked unavailable in `tools_available`.  
for tool_name, runner in [
    ("pyright", run_pyright),
    ("ruff", run_ruff),
    ("bandit", run_bandit),
    ("mypy", run_mypy),
]:
    if not tools_available.get(tool_name, True):
        continue  # already known unavailable
    try:
        diags = runner(existing)
        all_diags.extend(diags)
        tools_available[tool_name] = True
    except ToolNotFoundError as e:
        logger.warning("Tool not installed: %s", e)
        tools_available[tool_name] = False
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning("Tool %s failed: %s", tool_name, e)
        tools_available[tool_name] = False

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_categorise_pyright()` returns `DefectCategory.TYPE_SAFETY` as default for any pyright diagnostic. However, pyright also reports `"reportUnusedImport"` (dead code) and `"reportUnusedVariable"` (dead code). These are not type‑safety issues; they should be categorized as `DEAD_CODE`. The current heuristic misses these.  
FOLLOW: Mis‑categorization skews `counts_by_category`; dead‑code issues appear as type‑safety, misleading the insect brain about defect distribution.

FIND — `run_bandit()` maps severity `"LOW"` → `"info"`, `"MEDIUM"` → `"warning"`, `"HIGH"` → `"error"`. However, the endocrine layer’s `counts_by_severity` uses these strings; the insect brain may treat `"info"` as ignorable. Bandit’s `"LOW"` severity still indicates a security issue (e.g., `B101: assert_used`). Downgrading to `"info"` hides security findings from severity‑based filters.  
FOLLOW: Security issues may be overlooked because they are classified as `"info"`.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX — Map `"LOW"` → `"warning"`, `"MEDIUM"` → `"error"`, `"HIGH"` → `"error"` (or keep `"HIGH"` as `"error"`). This ensures security issues are not silently dropped.  
sev_map = {"LOW": "warning", "MEDIUM": "error", "HIGH": "error"}

all_findings.description:
FIND — The fix evaluation sandbox breaks completely because `_create_sandbox` only copies the specific files listed in `source_paths` into `tmpdir`. It omits project dependencies (causing `pyright` and `mypy` to emit artificial missing-import errors) and omits the test directory. When `evaluate_fix` runs `test_cmd` (e.g., `pytest bench/tests/`) with `cwd=tmpdir`, it fails to find the tests and exits with a non-zero code. Because `tests_passed` evaluates to `False` (or `net_type_errors > 0` due to import errors), `_compute_fix_verdict` erroneously rejects all valid fixes as `HARMFUL`.
FOLLOW: `_create_sandbox` copies only target files -> sandbox lacks tests and config -> `pytest` exits non-zero & pyright throws import errors -> `eval_result.tests_passed = False` -> verdict defaults to `HARMFUL` -> valid fixes rejected.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Modify `_create_sandbox` to copy the entire project directory into the sandbox, ensuring all tests and configurations are present. Replace the loop over `source_paths` with `shutil.copytree(os.getcwd(), tmpdir, dirs_exist_ok=True, ignore=shutil.ignore_patterns('.git', '__pycache__', 'venv', '.venv'))`. Calculate `patched_path` relative to `os.getcwd()` and overwrite the target file with `patched_text`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — Strategy 2 in `_apply_fix_to_source` is dangerously overbroad. It compiles the proposed fix, and if it's >5 lines of valid Python, treats it as a whole-file replacement. Because models routinely output standalone functions or classes as fixes (which compile perfectly), Strategy 2 silently replaces the entire source file (e.g., 800 lines) with a single 10-line snippet. This mutilates the file, triggering massive static analysis errors and guaranteeing the fix is rejected as `HARMFUL`.
FOLLOW: Model outputs a 15-line function replacement -> `compile()` succeeds -> file replaced with 15 lines -> `pyright` throws 100 missing variable errors -> `net_type_errors > 0` -> fix rejected as `HARMFUL`.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Remove Strategy 2 entirely, as models rarely output 800-line whole-file replacements. Alternatively, restrict it by adding a length check: `if fix.count('\n') > len(source_text.splitlines()) * 0.5: return fix`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — Strategy 3 (line-level replacement) fails when models enclose code fragments in markdown backticks (e.g., `Line 10: \`old_code\` -> \`new_code\``). The regex `r"[Ll]ines?\s+(\d+).*?:\s*(.+?)\s*->\s*(.+)"` captures the backticks into `old_frag` and `new_frag`. Since the actual source code does not contain these backticks, `old_frag in lines[start_line]` evaluates to `False`, and the replacement fails silently.
FOLLOW: Regex captures backticks -> `old_frag = "\`old_code\`"` -> `"\`old_code\`" in "old_code = 1"` is False -> replacement block bypassed -> `modified = False` -> fix fails to apply.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Strip backticks and quotes from the extracted fragments when assigning them. Change `old_frag = lm.group(3).strip()` to `old_frag = lm.group(3).strip().strip("\`'")` and `new_frag = lm.group(4).strip().strip("\`'")`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — Strategy 3 applies multi-line replacements sequentially. When replacing a multi-line range (`start_line != end_line`), it replaces a list slice with a single string element (`lines[start_line:end_line + 1] = [new_block]`). This shrinks the length of the `lines` list, shifting all subsequent line indices. If a fix contains multiple replacements (e.g., lines 10-15, then lines 20-25), the second replacement will use the original indices but hit the shifted code, missing its target and corrupting the file.
FOLLOW: Multi-line replacement shrinks `lines` list by $N$ elements -> next regex match uses original line index -> accesses index that now points to code $N$ lines further down -> `old_frag in block` evaluates to False or modifies wrong code.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Collect all `line_pattern.finditer(fix)` matches into a list, sort them in reverse order of line numbers, and apply them from bottom to top: `matches = list(line_pattern.finditer(fix)); matches.sort(key=lambda m: int(m.group(1)), reverse=True); for lm in matches: ...`

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_mypy()` cannot parse standard mypy diagnostics that omit a column number. The regex requires `file:line:col: severity: ...`, but mypy commonly emits `file.py:123: error: ...` unless column reporting is consistently present for that message. In this function, any non-matching line is silently dropped, so the health scan and fix evaluator undercount or fully miss mypy findings. Evidence: the parser pattern is `^(.+?):(\d+):(\d+):\s+(error|warning|note):...$`, which makes the column mandatory.
FOLLOW: Mypy is one of four advertised health-scan tools. If its output is partially or wholly discarded, `scan_health()` produces silently wrong totals and category counts, and `evaluate_fix()` can mark patches SAFE/NEUTRAL despite new mypy errors. This is HIGH in a PoC because the feature appears to run but yields misleading results.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Make the column group optional in the regex and default `column` to 0 when absent, e.g. accept both `file:line: error:` and `file:line:col: error:` formats.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` advertises comparison of “type checkers and linters” before/after, and the module-level health scan includes mypy, but fix evaluation never runs mypy at all. It only records pyright/ruff/bandit pre/post counts (`pre_type_errors`/`new_type_errors` come solely from `run_pyright`). Evidence: `evaluate_fix()` calls `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, ...)`, `_count_tool_issues(run_ruff, ...)`, `_count_tool_issues(run_bandit, ...)`; `run_mypy()` is unused in fix evaluation and there are no mypy fields in `FixEvaluation`.
FOLLOW: The endocrine layer can report a proposed fix SAFE even when it introduces mypy-only type regressions. That is silently wrong relative to the documented capability and inconsistent with `scan_health()`, which does run mypy. The gap is material because users will assume “type checkers” plural were applied.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Include mypy in pre/post fix evaluation and verdict computation by adding mypy issue counts to `FixEvaluation` and treating newly introduced mypy errors the same way as pyright regressions.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_create_sandbox()` can return a sandbox with no copy of the target file’s original package metadata files (`__init__.py`) when those files are not explicitly listed in `source_paths`. The function claims to preserve package structure, but it only copies listed files. Evidence: the copy loop iterates only `for src in source_paths`, then optionally writes `target_path`; no ancestor package files are copied.
FOLLOW: Even if sibling modules are present in `source_paths`, missing `__init__.py` files can change import resolution for tests and static analyzers inside the sandbox, causing false failures or different module identities than the live tree. This is a direct end-to-end defect in sandbox fidelity.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — When building the sandbox tree, also copy `__init__.py` files along the relative path from the common ancestor to each copied Python file.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` can emit a false `slow_model` signal for a single model run. With one timing entry, `median_duration` equals that model’s duration, making the relative threshold impossible (`rt.duration_s > median*2.5`), so slow-model detection is effectively dead for one model; with two models, using upper-middle median further weakens detection. Evidence: the function only compares against within-round median and has no minimum-sample guard or absolute fallback.
FOLLOW: The advertised pacing feature “timing ... monitoring” does not fire meaningfully on small model sets or degraded runs where only one or two models respond. That weakens the insect brain’s ability to react to slowdown exactly when failures reduce the population.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Require at least 3 timing samples for relative slow-model detection; otherwise skip emitting `slow_model` rather than implying the feature is operating.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` records pyright `severity` verbatim, but downstream aggregation expects normalized buckets shared with other tools. Pyright JSON commonly uses `"error"`, `"warning"`, and `"information"`, while the module docstrings and `ToolDiagnostic.severity` comment specify `"error", "warning", "info"`. Evidence: `severity_raw = diag.get("severity", "error")` is stored unchanged; no mapping from `"information"` to `"info"` exists.
FOLLOW: `counts_by_severity` becomes inconsistent across tools (`info` for bandit low, `information` for pyright info), so consumers reading aggregate severity totals receive split buckets for the same concept. This silently distorts health metrics and any thresholding built on them.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Normalize pyright severities on ingest, mapping `"information"` to `"info"` and passing through `"error"`/`"warning"`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()`/`run_ruff()`/`run_bandit()`/`run_mypy()` invoke tool binaries without setting `cwd` to the project root or the source tree root during `scan_health()`. They are called as `runner(existing)` from `scan_health()`, and each runner calls `_run_tool(cmd)` with `cwd=None`. These tools resolve config files (`pyrightconfig.json`, `ruff.toml`, Bandit exclusions, mypy config) and imports relative to working directory / project root. As written, health scans depend on whatever directory the orchestrator happened to launch from, not on the code under review.
FOLLOW: This makes the primary endocrine health signal nondeterministic and can silently produce wrong diagnostics counts or miss configured checks entirely. The insect brain consumes `health_scan` mechanically, so wrong counts propagate into trend analysis and human review. Fix evaluation partially avoids this by using `cwd=tmpdir` for tests, but health scan—the advertised between-round static analysis—can fire with the wrong config or none at all.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — In `scan_health()`, compute a stable analysis root from `existing` (e.g. common ancestor directory) and pass it as `cwd` to each tool runner; thread `cwd` through `run_pyright`, `run_ruff`, `run_bandit`, and `run_mypy` into `_run_tool`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_mypy()` ignores non-regex-parsed output and does not surface execution failure. It only checks `stderr == "NOT_FOUND"`. For timeout, `_run_tool()` returns `stderr="TIMEOUT"` and empty stdout; for config/import/internal errors, mypy can emit messages that do not match the single regex. The function then returns an empty diagnostics list with no failure signal.
FOLLOW: Health scans and fix evaluation can treat mypy failure as “no issues,” understating type-health and misclassifying bad fixes as safe. Because mypy is one of the four advertised health tools, a dead/non-firing mypy path means a significant feature does not actually fire cleanly end-to-end.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Mirror the pyright hard-failure handling: if `_run_tool()` returns `stderr in {"NOT_FOUND","TIMEOUT"}` or stdout lines are present but none parse, raise `ToolNotFoundError` for not found and otherwise raise/log an explicit tool-failure exception so callers mark the tool unavailable instead of returning `[]`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` never runs `mypy` before or after the patch, despite `mypy` being declared as a supported endocrine tool and used in health scans. Pre/post fields only track pyright, ruff, and bandit (`pre_type_errors`/`new_type_errors` come solely from `run_pyright`), and verdict computation ignores mypy entirely.
FOLLOW: A fix that introduces mypy-detectable type breakage but passes pyright can be marked SAFE/NEUTRAL. This is a silently wrong fix-evaluation result in the module’s key advertised capability. It also creates inconsistency between health scan and fix evaluation: one reports four tools, the other effectively evaluates three.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Add mypy counts to `FixEvaluation` and include `run_mypy` in pre/post issue counting and verdict computation, using the same scope as the other tools.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` stores zero-based line and character indices directly from pyright JSON (`range.start.line`, `range.start.character`) while `run_ruff()`, `run_bandit()`, and `run_mypy()` store one-based lines/columns. The module then aggregates diagnostics from all tools into one `HealthScan` without normalizing coordinate conventions.
FOLLOW: Cross-tool diagnostics in `HealthScan.diagnostics` are internally inconsistent. Any downstream consumer or reviewer comparing file/line counts or navigating to a reported pyright location will be off by one for pyright only. This degrades defect detection accuracy and can mislead fix targeting.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Normalize pyright coordinates to one-based values when constructing `ToolDiagnostic` (`line + 1`, `character + 1`), matching the other tool parsers.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` can emit `novelty_plateau` as early as round 2 because it uses `window = 3` and triggers when `len(novelty_counts) >= 3` and `round_idx >= 2`. In a PoC distributed review, three low-novelty rounds at startup are not a reliable convergence plateau; the signal can fire before the system has had enough time to exploit cross-round relay and immune feedback.
FOLLOW: The insect brain may mechanically interpret an early plateau as a cue to “check_convergence,” shortening exploration and risking premature termination while significant bugs remain. This is a wrong pacing trigger, not mere polish, because pacing signals are one of the four advertised endocrine outputs.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Add a minimum-round gate before plateau emission, e.g. require `round_idx >= 4` in addition to the 3-round window.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_mypy()` regex pattern does not handle Windows absolute paths (drive letter + colon). The pattern `^(.+?):` greedily matches the drive letter (e.g., `C:`) as part of the path, then the rest of the path until the next colon, breaking column/line parsing. Example: `C:\path\to\file.py:10:20: error: ...` incorrectly parses group1=`C`, group2=`\path\to\file.py`, group3=`10`. This makes all mypy diagnostics on Windows unparseable, silencing all type errors from Windows systems.  
FOLLOW: Without correct parsing, the endocrine layer reports zero mypy diagnostics on Windows, producing a false-clean health signal. The insect brain receives misleading metrics, potentially delaying convergence.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX — Update the regex in `run_mypy()` to handle optional drive letters:  
pattern = re.compile(
    r"^((?:[a-zA-Z]:)?[^:]+):(\d+):(\d+):\s+(error|warning|note):\s+(.+?)(?:\s+\[(.+?)\])?$"
)
This matches an optional drive letter (`[a-zA-Z]:`) followed by non‑colon path characters, then colon‑delimited line, column, severity, message, and optional code.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_create_sandbox()` fails when source paths are on different drives on Windows (e.g., `C:\a.py`, `D:\b.py`). `os.path.commonpath()` raises `ValueError: Paths don't have the same drive`. The endocrine layer crashes during fix evaluation, making the feature dead on Windows multi‑drive setups.  
FOLLOW: Fix evaluation crashes, returning `UNEVALUABLE` for all findings. The insect brain never receives fix‑evaluation signals, losing the key immune‑pipeline enhancement.

FIND — `scan_health()` silently swallows `json.JSONDecodeError` and `KeyError` in `run_pyright()`, `run_ruff()`, `run_bandit()`. If a tool outputs malformed JSON (e.g., truncated due to crash), the error is logged as warning but the function returns empty diagnostics. This hides tool failures from the health scan, presenting a false‑clean state.  
FOLLOW: A crashing pyright (e.g., segfault) produces empty stdout, JSON decode fails, zero diagnostics reported. The insect brain sees no type‑safety issues, missing critical code defects.

FIND — `_categorise_ruff()` classifies all `F` codes as `DefectCategory.DEAD_CODE` (`if code.startswith("F"): return DefectCategory.DEAD_CODE`). Pyflakes `F821` is "undefined name", which is a critical runtime crash, not dead code. Masking it as dead code leads to incorrect downstream prioritization.
FOLLOW: An undefined name bug will be tagged as DEAD_CODE. The insect brain and immune pipeline will treat it as a low-severity style/cleanup issue rather than a critical code behavioral bug, potentially ignoring it.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Check for critical F-codes explicitly before the prefix match. `if code == "F821": return DefectCategory.TYPE_SAFETY`

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_create_sandbox` uses `os.path.commonpath(all_paths)` as the base directory for copying files. If all source files are inside a package (e.g., `bench/`), `commonpath` evaluates to that package directory. The files are flattened into `tmpdir` without the package prefix (e.g., `tmpdir/endocrine.py` instead of `tmpdir/bench/endocrine.py`).
FOLLOW: Static analysis tools (pyright/mypy) running in the sandbox will fail to resolve absolute imports like `from bench.dm import...` because the `bench` directory no longer exists in the sandbox root. This introduces artificial type errors, causing `_compute_fix_verdict` to erroneously mark nearly all SAFE fixes as HARMFUL.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Use the project root (current working directory) instead of `commonpath`. Replace `common = os.path.commonpath(all_paths)` with `common = os.getcwd()`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_apply_fix_to_source` Strategy 3 regex (`line_pattern`) uses `.+?` and `.+` without `re.DOTALL`. Because the dot metacharacter does not match newlines by default, the regex will fail to capture any replacement blocks where the `old_frag` or `new_frag` spans multiple lines.
FOLLOW: Models frequently output multi-line code blocks in replacements. The regex will silently fail to match them, returning `None`, and `evaluate_fix` will mark the fix `UNEVALUABLE`, leaving the bug unfixed.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Add `re.DOTALL` to `line_pattern` and make the final match non-greedy, bounded by a lookahead: `re.compile(r"[Ll]ines?\s+(\d+)(?:\s*[-–]\s*(\d+))?:\s*(.*?)\s*->\s*(.*?)(?=\n[Ll]ines?|\Z)", re.DOTALL)`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — In `compute_pacing_signals()`, the response size anomaly check (Check 4) incorrectly hardcodes `signal_type="context_growth"`. 
FOLLOW: This overwrites or conflates the true context growth signal (Check 2). The insect brain relies on distinct `signal_type` values to trigger different mechanical mitigations. Sending a response size anomaly as a context growth signal will trigger the wrong downstream reaction (e.g., degrading relay instead of isolating a broken model).
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Change `signal_type="context_growth"` to `signal_type="response_size_anomaly"` in Check 4.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals` signal #4 (response size anomaly, line ~510) reuses `signal_type="context_growth"`, the same string as signal #2 (context budget warning, line ~480). The insect brain receives `PacingSignal` objects and dispatches on `signal_type` — it cannot distinguish "context budget at 85%" from "one model produced 50k chars". Both suggest `"degrade_relay"` but require different remediation: budget pressure calls for summary mode across all models, while a single verbose model calls for per-model truncation.

FOLLOW: The insect brain's pacing signal consumer (if it exists) treats both signals identically. If the brain eventually implements automated response to `context_growth` signals, it would degrade all models when only one is verbose, or truncate a single model when the entire context is overflowing. For PoC, pacing signals are logged for human review, so the consequence is misleading logs rather than wrong automated action. However, once the brain acts on pacing signals, this becomes a silent wrong-action bug.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
# Signal #4: change signal_type to distinguish from budget pressure
signals.append(PacingSignal(
    signal_type="response_size_anomaly",
    ...

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` does not sandbox the interpreter used for tests. In Stage "Run tests if command provided", it executes `_run_tool(test_cmd, timeout=_TOOL_TIMEOUT, cwd=tmpdir)`. In context, the immune pipeline calls `evaluate_fixes(..., test_cmd=["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...])`. Changing `cwd` to `tmpdir` does not force `python3` to import the sandboxed package tree; Python still prepends the current working directory, but whether the sandboxed `bench` is imported depends on invocation path and environment. More importantly, the module defines `PYTHON_313` specifically but never uses it here, so tests may run under whatever `python3` is on PATH, not the same interpreter/tool environment the endocrine layer assumes. That makes fix evaluation verdicts environment-dependent and can silently mark a fix SAFE/HARMFUL based on the wrong interpreter.
FOLLOW: Downstream, `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()` marks findings `verified=True` when fix evaluation returns SAFE or NEUTRAL. If tests run under a different interpreter/environment than the bench’s configured toolchain, the bug-closed gate can close real bugs or reject valid fixes based on non-bench conditions. This is a silently wrong result in a core coordination path, not just a quality issue.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — When `test_cmd` is provided, replace a leading `"python"`/`"python3"` executable with `PYTHON_313` before invoking `_run_tool`, so sandbox tests run under the same configured interpreter/tool environment as the rest of the endocrine layer.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` and `run_bandit()` treat empty or unparsable stdout as “no diagnostics” instead of tool failure. In `run_pyright()`, any JSON parse failure is caught, only a warning is logged, and `[]` is returned. In `run_bandit()`, `json.loads(result.stdout) if result.stdout.strip() else {}` makes empty stdout equivalent to zero findings. `_run_tool()` encodes timeout as `stderr="TIMEOUT"` with `returncode=-1`, but only `NOT_FOUND` is promoted to an exception. This fail-open behavior remains for bandit and for pyright parse failures, unlike the already-registered C0009 which is specific to pyright timeout handling.
FOLLOW: In `scan_health()`, failed tools are marked available if no exception is raised, so health scans can report a healthy system with `tools_available["bandit"]=True` or `["pyright"]=True` while the tool actually timed out or emitted unusable output. In `evaluate_fix()`, `_count_tool_issues()` then sees `0` issues and can classify harmful fixes as SAFE/NEUTRAL. This directly corrupts both health monitoring and fix verification.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — In each runner, treat `result.returncode == -1`, `stderr == "TIMEOUT"`, and JSON parse failure/empty stdout for JSON-output tools as tool execution failure by raising `ToolNotFoundError`-like failure or a dedicated exception, so callers mark the tool unavailable instead of returning an empty diagnostic list.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `scan_health(source_paths)` is documented to accept “Absolute paths to Python source files to analyse”, but it passes those absolute file paths directly to pyright/mypy/ruff/bandit without setting `cwd` or normalizing against project config. For tools whose behavior depends on config discovery from project root, running them from an arbitrary process cwd against absolute paths can bypass repository-local config files (`pyrightconfig.json`, `mypy.ini`, Ruff config, Bandit config) unless the current process happened to start at the project root. The module already encodes absolute binary paths and sandbox logic, so this unstated dependency on external cwd is an interface bug.
FOLLOW: Health scan outputs become non-reproducible across orchestrator launch locations. The insect brain consumes these metrics mechanically; inconsistent counts affect convergence/pacing decisions and human review. In fix evaluation this also compounds the pre/post comparability problem because tool behavior can change with caller cwd rather than source state.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Compute a deterministic project root from `source_paths` and pass it as `cwd` to all tool invocations in both health scan and fix evaluation.

all_findings.description:
FIND — The advertised defect category `RACE_CONDITION` is effectively dead for actual health scanning. `scan_health()` only gathers diagnostics from pyright, ruff, bandit, and mypy. Of those, only `_categorise_ruff()` can emit `RACE_CONDITION`, and only via message-keyword heuristics (`"race"`, `"concurrent"`, `"thread"`, `"lock"`). Ruff diagnostics for concurrency bugs generally surface as rule codes, not human messages containing those words. Pyright/mypy/bandit categorisers never emit `RACE_CONDITION`. So one of the documented defect-detect categories is practically unreachable.
FOLLOW: The endocrine layer claims defect detection across categories including race conditions, and the insect brain may interpret category counts as meaningful signals. In practice this category will stay zero even when tools report relevant issues, misleading reviewers about feature coverage. For PoC this is a silent completeness failure of a named feature.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Remove `RACE_CONDITION` from the declared defect categories for this PoC unless a concrete tool/rule mapping is implemented; simplest sufficient correction is to align the declared categories with what the tool runners can actually emit.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` silently drops all diagnostics when pyright exits non-zero with valid JSON only on `stdout` absent or malformed, because parse failure is only logged and returns `[]` (`except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError): logger.warning(...)`). Pyright commonly returns structured failure information via non-success exit or stderr on config/environment errors. In this module, that becomes indistinguishable from “no issues found,” causing the health scan to report a clean state even when the tool failed to analyze.
FOLLOW: `scan_health()` treats any normal return from `run_pyright()` as `tools_available["pyright"] = True` and aggregates zero diagnostics. That feeds incorrect health signals to the insect brain, masks analyzer failure in the report, and corrupts fix evaluation because `_count_tool_issues(run_pyright, ...)` also interprets the same failure mode as zero new type errors. A broken pyright invocation can therefore produce both false-clean health scans and false SAFE/NEUTRAL fix verdicts.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — In `run_pyright()`, treat non-JSON output or `returncode == -1`/timeout as tool failure, not empty diagnostics: raise `ToolNotFoundError` for missing binary and raise a normal exception (or dedicated parse/tool-failure exception) when output cannot be parsed or the process times out, so callers mark the tool unavailable/failed instead of “0 findings.”

all_findings.description:
FIND — `evaluate_fix()` runs tests in the sandbox with `_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)` but does not rewrite the executable path itself. The immune pipeline passes `test_cmd=["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]` from context. In a multi-interpreter setup, this invokes whatever `python3` is on PATH, not the same 3.13 toolchain hardcoded for pyright/ruff/bandit/mypy, and not necessarily the interpreter expected by the copied sandbox environment. This creates an interface mismatch between endocrine fix evaluation and immune pipeline assumptions.
FOLLOW: Even if test path rewriting bugs are fixed elsewhere, tests can still run under a different interpreter than the static analyzers and source environment. A fix may appear SAFE because tests pass under the wrong interpreter, or HARMFUL because pytest/imports fail under an unintended interpreter, producing misleading verification signals that the immune pipeline uses to set `verified=True`.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Before running `test_cmd`, rewrite a leading bare `"python"`/`"python3"` executable to `PYTHON_313` so the test subprocess uses the same interpreter family as the rest of the endocrine toolchain.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_compute_fix_verdict()` marks a fix SAFE whenever `tests_passed is True`, even if no diagnostic counts improved and even if the target bug was not actually affected. The code path is: after rejecting positive net deltas, it computes `total_net`; if `total_net < 0` return SAFE; then `if result.tests_passed is True: return "SAFE"`; else NEUTRAL. That means “tests happened to pass” upgrades a no-op patch to SAFE.
FOLLOW: In the immune pipeline, `run_immune_pipeline()` marks findings `verified=True` for `SAFE` or `NEUTRAL`, but the SAFE label still matters as the endocrine layer’s direct output and may be consumed by humans or future logic as stronger evidence than NEUTRAL. Mislabeling no-op or irrelevant fixes as SAFE degrades trust in fix evaluation and can prematurely close bugs if consumers later distinguish SAFE from NEUTRAL.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — In `_compute_fix_verdict()`, only return SAFE when tests pass and at least one issue count improves (`total_net < 0`); if tests pass with `total_net == 0`, return NEUTRAL.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` novelty plateau threshold and emitted metric are internally inconsistent. The condition is `all(n <= 1 for n in recent)`, but the emitted signal uses `threshold=float(window)` where `window = 3`. The actual decision boundary is “every round in the last 3 had novelty <=1”; the recorded threshold says “3”. This metadata does not describe the trigger that fired.
FOLLOW: The insect brain receives pacing signals as structured control data. If a novelty plateau signal says `metric_value=2.0 threshold=3.0`, downstream logging or dashboards imply a sum-based comparison, but the actual predicate was per-round. This can mislead human review and any downstream logic that inspects `metric_value`/`threshold` rather than recomputing from `detail`.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Set the novelty plateau signal metadata to match the real predicate, e.g. `metric_value=float(max(recent))` and `threshold=1.0`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — The advertised “defect detection” capability is still incomplete at the coordinator level even beyond the already-registered missing public API. `scan_health()` only aggregates raw category counts from tool diagnostics; it never produces the documented defect categories “off-by-one, race conditions, security, dead code” as a distinct stage output or report field separate from tool output. `EndocrineReport` has `health_scan`, `fix_evaluations`, and `pacing_signals`, but no defect-detection result object.
FOLLOW: The module claims four endocrine functions, but consumers only receive tool diagnostics plus counts. Even if a helper API is later added, the coordinator currently does not expose defect detection as part of the inter-round report handed to the insect brain. This leaves one documented feature effectively non-firing in the real integration path.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Add a `defect_summary` field to `EndocrineReport` and populate it in `EndocrineLayer.run()` using the existing diagnostic categories/counts, without extra inference complexity.

all_findings.description:
FIND — The tool runners `run_ruff`, `run_bandit`, and `run_mypy` only check for `stderr == "NOT_FOUND"` to raise `ToolNotFoundError`. They ignore timeouts (stderr == "TIMEOUT") and will attempt to parse the empty or partial output, returning an empty diagnostic list and marking the tool as available in the health scan. This leads to silently missing diagnostics and incorrect health signals.
FOLLOW: The issue is identical to C0009 (confirmed for `run_pyright`). Without the fix, a timeout in any of these tools will be treated as a successful run with no issues, potentially hiding real problems. The health scan will report fewer errors than actually exist, misleading the insect brain’s pacing and convergence decisions.

FIND — `evaluate_fix()` has no `except` block surrounding the sandbox creation and tool execution logic. If `_create_sandbox()` encounters an `OSError` (e.g., file copy failure, permission denied, or target write failure), the exception escapes the function entirely.
FOLLOW: The unhandled exception propagates to `evaluate_fixes()`, and subsequently out to `EndocrineLayer.run()`. This completely crashes the orchestration loop, halting the current round and preventing the insect brain from receiving pacing signals or transitioning to the next phase.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Wrap the sandbox creation and post-fix analysis logic inside a `try...except Exception as e:` block. On catch, set `eval_result.verdict = "UNEVALUABLE"` and `eval_result.apply_error = f"Sandbox error: {e}"`, ensuring safe isolation.

all_findings.description:
FIND — In `run_pyright`, `run_ruff`, and `run_bandit`, JSON objects are parsed using chained dictionary `.get(key, {})` lookups. If the tool's JSON output explicitly contains `null` for these keys (e.g., `{"range": null}` or `{"location": null}`), `.get()` returns `None`. Subsequent chained lookups (like `None.get("start")`) raise an `AttributeError`, and iteration raises `TypeError`. These exceptions are NOT caught by the adjacent `except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError):` blocks.
FOLLOW: The `AttributeError` or `TypeError` propagates up to `scan_health()`, where the generic `except Exception:` block catches it, logs a tool failure, and permanently sets the tool's availability to `False`. This silently disables critical verification tools for the remainder of the scan, generating false "zero defects" signals that deceive the system.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Expand the exception handlers in the tool runners to catch `(json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, AttributeError, TypeError)`, or explicitly use the logical OR fallback: `loc = issue.get("location") or {}`.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_categorise_pyright` (lines ~170–178) uses substring keyword matching that produces systematic miscategorisation. The keyword `"none"` matches any message containing the substring "none", including messages like `"None of the overloads for '__getitem__' matched"` (TYPE_SAFETY, not NULL_DEREF) and `"expression has type 'None | str'"` (TYPE_SAFETY context). The keyword `"is not callable"` routes to NULL_DEREF but describes a TYPE_SAFETY condition (calling a non-callable type, not dereferencing None). The match order means NULL_DEREF captures many TYPE_SAFETY diagnostics because `"none"` appears in type error messages about Optional types. Evidence: the third condition (`"type"`, `"incompatible"`, `"cannot assign"`, `"argument"`) is never reached when the message also contains `"none"` — and most Optional-related type errors contain `"none"`.
FOLLOW: `counts_by_category` in HealthScan is skewed: NULL_DEREF inflated, TYPE_SAFETY deflated. `health_trend()` shows false null-deref trends. The insect brain (or orchestrator) acting on category counts would misdiagnose the code's health profile. In the immune pipeline, if category counts influence finding triage or priority, the bias propagates. The magnitude is proportional to how many pyright diagnostics mention "None" — in a typical Python codebase with Optional types, this is substantial (estimated 30–50% of pyright diagnostics mention "None" or "Optional").

FIND — Pacing signals are computed but have no consumer in the insect brain interface. `EndocrineLayer.run()` calls `compute_pacing_signals()` which requires three external inputs: `round_timings` (List[RoundTiming]), `novelty_counts` (List[int]), and `cumulative_context_chars` (int). All three default to empty/zero in `EndocrineLayer.run()` signature. The insect brain (`InsectBrain`) has no attribute, method, or code path that reads pacing signals from an `EndocrineReport`. The docstring claims `brain.endocrine_report = report` but `InsectBrain.check_convergence()` references only `self.conv_detector` — it never reads endocrine data. Combined effect: unless the orchestrator (a) constructs `RoundTiming` objects from per-model dispatch data, (b) extracts `novel_count` from brain metrics and accumulates it into a list, (c) tracks cumulative context chars, AND (d) acts on the returned pacing signals independently of the brain — all four pacing signal types (`slow_model`, `context_growth`, `novelty_plateau`, `response_size_anomaly`) silently never fire.
FOLLOW: If pacing signals never fire, the endocrine layer provides only health scan + fix evaluation. The "timing, context growth, novelty plateau monitoring" advertised in the module docstring is dead feature space. For the PoC, this means: (1) a slow model is never detected and timeout is never increased, (2) context budget exhaustion is never signalled for graceful degradation, (3) novelty plateau (convergence signal) from the endocrine layer is never emitted. The brain's own convergence detection (kappa) partially compensates for (3) but not for (1) or (2).

FIND — `health_trend()` (lines ~620–635) returns per-category diagnostic counts across rounds but does not include tool availability data per scan. When a tool is intermittently unavailable (e.g., pyright binary temporarily missing, or `ToolNotFoundError` caught in `scan_health`), that scan records zero diagnostics for that tool's categories. The trend data shows the category count dropping to zero then recovering — indistinguishable from the code actually improving then regressing.
FOLLOW: Any consumer using `health_trend()` to detect code quality changes (improving/degrading) would misinterpret tool outages as code changes. In the PoC, if `health_trend()` is not called by any consumer (I cannot find a caller in the provided code), this is dead code and the bug is latent. If the orchestrator calls it, the bug produces silently wrong trend analysis.

FIND — `EndocrineLayer.run()` returns an `EndocrineReport` containing `fix_evaluations`, but `bench/insect_brain.py` exposes no endocrine integration point at all. There is no `endocrine_report` field on `BrainState` or `RoundRecord`, no import of `EndocrineReport`, and no method that accepts or persists endocrine output. This contradicts the endocrine docstring claim “Assembled by EndocrineLayer.report() and handed to the insect brain” and the task statement that endocrine pacing/health signals guide round decisions. Evidence in context: `EndocrineLayer.run()` produces the report; `InsectBrain` never consumes it.
FOLLOW: The endocrine layer’s core outputs are effectively dead at the system boundary: health scan, fix evaluation verdicts, and pacing signals may run, but the insect brain cannot receive, persist, or act on them. For PoC goals, this means the advertised “whole-body health monitor” feature does not fire end-to-end; reviewers would be misled into thinking endocrine feedback affects orchestration when it currently cannot.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Add a minimal integration slot in `InsectBrain`, e.g. `self.endocrine_report: Optional[EndocrineReport] = None`, and have the orchestrator assign the report there between rounds. No extra processing is needed; just make the interface exist so the feature can actually be handed off.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `_count_tool_issues()` is annotated and documented to accept a single `file_path: str`, but `run_pyright`, `run_ruff`, and `run_bandit` all require `List[str]`. The function currently calls `tool_runner([file_path])`, so the implementation is correct, but the interface contract is wrong. This is not just notation: the same helper is reused as the abstraction boundary for fix evaluation, and its current signature invites future callers to pass a list or alternative scope incorrectly. The mismatch is visible directly in the function definition versus the runner signatures.
FOLLOW: This helper is central to fix evaluation. A misleading contract at this boundary increases the chance of future regressions where callers pass already-listified paths or assume single-file semantics while tool runners have project-scope behavior. Because fix evaluation already has multiple scope/path bugs, this incorrect helper contract compounds maintenance risk and can reintroduce silently wrong verdicts.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Change `_count_tool_issues` to accept `paths: List[str]` and pass `tool_runner(paths)` directly, updating call sites accordingly.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_mypy()` drops valid mypy diagnostics when column numbers are absent. Its regex hard-requires `file:line:col: severity: message`, but mypy commonly emits `file:line: error: ...` without a column, depending on message type/options. The current parser therefore undercounts or returns zero diagnostics for valid output forms. Evidence: the compiled pattern is `^(.+?):(\d+):(\d+):\s+(error|warning|note): ...$`, making the `:(\d+)` column segment mandatory.
FOLLOW: Health scans and fix evaluations can silently miss mypy findings, causing `counts_by_tool["mypy"]`, `total`, and category aggregates to be wrong. Because the module presents itself as mechanically extracting metrics, silently discarding a normal mypy output format produces misleading health reports and can falsely mark fixes as harmless.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Make the column group optional in the regex and set `column=0` when absent.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `compute_pacing_signals()` can emit a false `novelty_plateau` when `round_idx` and `novelty_counts` are inconsistent. The code comments say they “should track 1:1 with rounds”, but the actual guard only checks `len(novelty_counts) >= 3 and round_idx >= 2`, then uses `recent = novelty_counts[-3:]` regardless of whether the latest list entry corresponds to `round_idx`. If the caller passes stale or extra history, the function silently evaluates the wrong rounds.
FOLLOW: A stale plateau signal can cause premature convergence checking or relay degradation decisions at the wrong time. In PoC terms this can make the pacing feature fire, but on the wrong evidence, misleading reviewers about convergence behavior.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — Require exact alignment before evaluating: only run the plateau check when `len(novelty_counts) == round_idx + 1`; otherwise skip emitting the signal.

all_findings.description:
FIND — `run_pyright()` silently drops all diagnostics when pyright exits nonzero with valid-but-partial JSON on stdout and any non-empty stderr. The code only treats `stderr == "NOT_FOUND"` as exceptional, otherwise it attempts `json.loads(result.stdout)` and, on parse failure, logs a warning then returns `[]`. Pyright commonly emits config/import/runtime errors via stderr while also failing the JSON contract; this path is interpreted as “no diagnostics”. Evidence: `run_pyright()` has no returncode check, no `TIMEOUT` handling beyond the generic parse failure, and no error sentinel; `scan_health()` then aggregates an empty list as a healthy tool result.
FOLLOW: This creates silently wrong health scans: type-check failures disappear from `HealthScan.total`, `counts_by_tool`, and `counts_by_category`. Because `evaluate_fix()` also uses `run_pyright()` via `_count_tool_issues()`, fix evaluation can mark broken fixes as SAFE/NEUTRAL when pyright actually failed to run or report. That directly undermines two advertised endocrine features: health scan and fix evaluation.
all_findings.proposed_fix: FIX — In `run_pyright()`, treat `result.returncode == -1`, `result.stderr == "TIMEOUT"`, empty/non-JSON stdout on nonzero exit, or JSON parse failure as tool failure by raising `RuntimeError` (or `ToolNotFoundError` only for NOT_FOUND). Do not return `[]` on parse failure.
